children.text: Travellers who fail at food in Egypt are not few.
Not because Egyptian food is weak. Quite the opposite. Koshari, ful, ta'amiya, mulukhiyah, stuffed pigeon, grilled fish, om ali, karkadeh. Egypt has strong everyday food, rooted in daily life.
The problem is that many travellers don't eat it.
Hotel buffets, safe international menus made for tourists, the same grilled plate in every city. End a trip on those alone and the Egyptian table looks dull.
In truth, to eat well in Egypt, you need a logic for each place. In
Cairo
, eat the city's food. In
Alexandria
, eat fish. In
Aswan
, get close to the Nubian table. In
Luxor
, use hotels and small west-bank places in combination. In the Red Sea, understand the resort's limits.
A small choice of where to eat changes the trip a lot.
The basics of Egyptian food
Egyptian food is not flashy food.

Rice, beans, lentils, bread, vegetables, herbs, chicken, pigeon, fish, lamb, beef. The ingredients are everyday. Flavour comes from oil, garlic, cumin, coriander, lemon, vinegar, tomato, chilli, and stock.
Koshari is rice, pasta, lentils, chickpeas, tomato sauce, and fried onions layered together. Too complete to call poor food, too everyday to call national food. Best eaten at a specialist shop.
Ful is stewed fava beans. The centre of breakfast — eaten with bread, oil, lemon, cumin, vegetables, egg. To know Egyptian morning, choose ful over the hotel omelette.
Ta'amiya is the Egyptian version of falafel. Often made with fava rather than chickpeas, deep green, lightly fried. A breakfast and a lunch.
Mulukhiyah is a green soup made with jute leaves. Slightly thick — a small surprise on a first try. With chicken or rabbit stock and garlic, it has a depth that feels Egyptian.
Hamam mahshi is pigeon stuffed with rice or freekeh. Small, intense, one of Egypt's celebratory dishes.
Om ali is a hot dessert of pastry, milk, nuts, and cream baked together. Sweet, heavy, worth eating once at the trip's end.
Karkadeh is a hibiscus drink. Cold or hot, both work. In Aswan and at the Nubian table, it appears naturally.
Eating in Cairo
Cairo is Egypt's most wide-ranging food city.
Fine dining is here. Hotel dining is here. Terraces along the Nile are here. But Cairo's real strength is in the layer of everyday food.
Eat koshari at a specialist shop. Fast turnover, many customers, a menu of basically only koshari — that kind of shop is best. As an entry to Egyptian food, this is the clearest.
Eat ful and ta'amiya in the morning. Neighbourhood places, local breakfast spots, old chains and corner shops. An Egyptian morning utterly unlike the hotel breakfast.

For traditional Egyptian food eaten in calm, restaurants in Zamalek, Downtown, or along the Nile are good — order mulukhiyah, pigeon, kofta, stuffed vegetables, and mezze. For a first traveller, places that can explain dishes are more comfortable.

For fine dining, Cairo has choices. Separate "food that feels Egyptian" from "international hotel fine dining." A Nile-view restaurant pays much in view; for food alone, smaller specialist places are often more interesting.
The trick in Cairo is splitting the day. Ful and ta'amiya in the morning. Koshari at lunch. A proper Egyptian dinner or a Nile-side meal at night. Just this shows the city's flavour.
Eating fish in Alexandria
In Alexandria, you should eat fish.

Alexandria as a Mediterranean city has a different food sense from Cairo. The sea is close, seafood is everyday, and cooking is relatively straightforward. Choose the fish, decide grilled or fried, eat it with salad, tahini, bread, rice.
Here, freshness matters more than complex cooking. A single grilled fish at a proper fish house can stay with you longer than a fancier plate.

Corniche restaurants for tourists work; the local fish houses with many local customers are often stronger. Choose a place where you can see fresh fish and pick it, a busy place, a coastal place with turnover.
The Alexandria meal is an entry into Mediterranean Egypt. A different Egypt from the country of pyramids and temples — port, fish, wind, cafés.
Eating in Luxor
Luxor is a site city, not a food city.

So calibrate expectations correctly. It isn't as wide as Cairo. Fish isn't as strong as Alexandria. But using a good hotel restaurant, a Nile terrace, and a small west-bank place in combination, you eat well enough.
On the east bank, hotel and Corniche-area restaurants are easy to use. After tiring sightseeing, the value of a place you can eat without worry is real.
On the west bank, meals are quieter. Around
Medinet Habu
and in village restaurants, food can come closer to home Egyptian cooking. Not lavish, but a time that fits the west bank.
What matters in Luxor is not making lunch too light. The
Valley of the Kings
and Karnak from the morning take real strength. In the hot season especially, build meals and hydration into the itinerary.
After evening
Luxor Temple
, eat by the Nile. Or watch sunset on the west bank and have a quiet dinner. In Luxor, choosing a place that fits the rhythm of sightseeing matters more than the meal itself.
Aswan and the Nubian table
In Aswan, get close to Nubian food.
The Nile, the islands, Nubian villages, hibiscus, spices, grilled fish, rice dishes, a slow meal. The Aswan meal is softer than Cairo or Luxor, with the air of the south.

Around Gharb Soheil and the Nubian villages, there are tourist places and places that serve Nubian food. Grilled fish, chicken or meat tagine, rice, vegetables, karkadeh. Closer to the food of the land than a polished restaurant.
Elephantine Island
has small guesthouses and restaurants. Eating while looking at the Nile fits the Aswan trip.

A meal on a high-end hotel terrace also has meaning in Aswan. Watching the First Cataract, Elephantine Island, and the desert hills while eating — the place is part of the experience, not just the food. That said, hotel operations and restaurant names change; confirm current status before booking.
What to avoid in Aswan is eating in a hurry. Here, even meals are a little slow on purpose.
Eating at a Red Sea resort
Red Sea meals depend on the resort.
In
Hurghada
El Gouna
, Sharm el-Sheikh, and
Marsa Alam
, many travellers eat inside the hotel. All-inclusive buffets, theme restaurants, beach grills, seafood night. Convenient, but not where you get deep into Egypt's food culture.
Resort food varies sharply by hotel. When choosing a hotel, check food reputation alongside room and beach. A few nights is fine; a week makes monotony tell.
El Gouna is the easiest area to use restaurants outside the hotel. With marina and town options, it suits families and couples who don't want to lock themselves into all-inclusive.
Marsa Alam has fewer non-hotel options. It is a sea-led place; food depends heavily on the hotel's quality. Confirm this before booking.
On the Red Sea, you'll want fish. Fresh grilled fish is a good choice, but resort menus can include imported or frozen fish. Ask after small local fish or the day's recommendation.
How to eat street food
Egyptian street food is not something to avoid.
But there is a way to choose.
Choose busy places. Choose places with turnover. Eat things cooked hot. Be careful with raw vegetables, ice, and anything washed in tap water. Be especially careful with seafood away from the coast.
Koshari, ful, ta'amiya, shawarma, grilled meat, bread, sweets. With chosen places, these are well within reach for travellers too.

You don't need to try everything from day one. Be a little careful in the first half of the trip; once your body adjusts, widen. People with sensitive stomachs shouldn't push it. Eating well in Egypt is not the same as eating everything.
Good for vegetarians too
Egypt suits vegetarians quite well.
Ful, ta'amiya, koshari, lentil soup, stuffed vegetables, salads, bread, mezze. Many dishes are meatless, and the Coptic fasting tradition has fed a culture of plant-based eating.

Vegans can also eat surprisingly easily in street food. In hotels and fine dining, options can paradoxically narrow into an international "vegetarian menu." Local food is sometimes more naturally plant-based.
What to confirm: butter, ghee, chicken stock, meat stock. To avoid these completely, say so clearly.
Drinks and sweets
In Egypt, drinks are part of the trip.
Tea is everywhere. Mint tea is common. Coffee runs from thick Turkish-style to modern-café espresso.
Karkadeh, especially in Aswan, is one to drink. Cold hibiscus works very well on a hot day.
Sugarcane juice is common at city juice stands. Fresh, sweet, and very Egyptian. Choose by hygiene.
For sweets: om ali, basbousa, kunafa, baklava, roz bi laban. Egyptian sweets are sweet. Eat in small amounts.
Alcohol is served at hotels, licensed restaurants, and some bars. Not at ordinary local eateries or street stalls. The Egyptian meal is easier when not built around alcohol.
What to eat where
In Cairo: ful, ta'amiya, koshari, traditional Egyptian dishes.
In Alexandria: fish and seafood.
In Luxor: hotel and west-bank meals that match sightseeing rhythm.
In Aswan: Nubian food, karkadeh, meals with a Nile view.
On the Red Sea: choose hotels well, simple meals by the sea.
Just this lifts Egyptian food considerably.
To eat well in Egypt
In Egypt, you don't need to chase a perfect restaurant list.

What matters more is eating in a way that fits the place. Eat the city's food in Cairo. Eat fish in Alexandria. Get close to the southern table in Aswan. In Luxor, eat without pushing past the tiredness of sightseeing.
Egyptian food is not made to be shown off.
It is food made to feed people.
So the good meals are often less about lavish plates than about the right place and the right time.
To eat well in Egypt, knowing that is enough.

deck: How to choose what to eat, and where, in Cairo, Alexandria, Luxor, Aswan, and the Red Sea — a practical food guide.
